html:
On 22 August 1639 Francis Day of the English East India Company was granted a strip of beach on the Coromandel coast by a local governor of the fading Vijayanagara kingdom. The fort built there, Fort St George, grew into Madras, now Chennai. It was the first of the three great cities the Company founded in India.

The Company wanted cotton cloth. The villages nearby wove the painted and printed cottons that sold in Southeast Asia and, more and more, in Europe (see Indian calicoes). The site had no harbour; ships anchored offshore and boats carried goods through the surf.

The fort was finished in 1644. Outside its walls grew "Black Town", where weavers, dyers and Indian merchants settled, drawn by low duties. By 1700 the town held perhaps 100,000 people.

In 1746 the French took Madras, and gave it back three years later by treaty. The wars that followed made the Company a land power in the south (see the Carnatic Wars). Robert Clive began here as a clerk.

Madras became the capital of a province covering most of south India. Bombay followed in 1668 (see Mumbai) and Calcutta in 1690. The city was renamed Chennai in 1996.
